chapter: New York 1930s and New Orleans expatriates
title: Sitting in around New York and Adrian's Tap Room
summary: Kmen sat in at Nick's and Adrian's Tap Room; recalls Artie Drillinger and Lyman Bunk.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Well did you play at Dick's? There's a regular number? No, no, no.
But I played there often. Often sat in?
Yeah, very often. Was it common for people to sit in there?

Well, no, but you see I had known all these guys so well, and the horn I played didn't get in anybody's way. To throw a tenor in with a Dixie group like that didn't hurt anything. I took pains that it didn't. And it meant that I got a chance to blow choruses with them, and I did blow a lot of them. It was a good way to practice and also to get yourself known by other musicians, because there were a lot of musicians that hung around. You almost had to do that sort of to break in in New York and get around and play whatever way you could. And I followed coming from the country to New York City. This was the one sure way. You get your horn out and get in and play. I played in places like Adrian's Tap Room always sitting in, you see. And Nixon, plenty of other places.
Who was at Adrian's Tap Room then?

There was a little four piece group. One thing I remember, Willie Lyon Smith was playing there on the single piano. And this little four piece group had a bass and a tenor sax. And Adrian would often play vibes with it, but he was also busy managing. He wasn't always on the bandstand. And I believe the piano, probably drums. And the tenor sax who was working there at the time I used to sit in was Artie Drillinger, D-R-I-L-L, Drillinger. And he's still around. He's somewhere, I think he's up in the studios now. He's still playing. He blew with a lot of good bands.
And he was a hot man there though.

Yes, well almost everybody in that period that came in was a hot man. But a lot of guys found out they weren't hot enough and then they became more legit or something. For instance, I had a fellow that came to New York with me and I had room for a while. He was from Cortland, New York, which is near Syracuse. And he played so hot in the Casco Mountains that we called it the nearest thing to a torrent or trumpet that we'd ever heard. And he still played a lot of jazz, but he made his biggest mark playing in bands like the Barnett Band and the Bob Crosby Band as the high trumpet man. Because when he played with Crosby for instance, Yank Lawson was also playing. Yank just played a little bit better jazz. And my friend is Lyman Bunk, his name was, he did have a tremendous lip, so he played the high trumpet parts. And this happened to many people that developed into lead men and developed into good double men playing many instruments, multiple instruments. They all could play some jazz, but just some of the fellows were specialists in it because they were better jazz men.
